title: Unit cost, break-even and setting your price

say: Unit cost, break-even, and setting your price.
This is the video for Module 2 of Pricing, Costing and Profit Planning.
Unit cost is what it costs you to make and sell one item. Here is the four-step method.
First, list every variable cost for one batch, with its quantity and current price.

panel.heading: Full cost of one unit
items: List every variable cost for one batch
Divide by good units: variable cost per unit
Divide monthly fixed costs by average sales
Add the two: full cost per unit

say: Second, add them and divide by the number of good units the batch gives.

panel.heading: Full cost of one unit
items: List every variable cost for one batch
Divide by good units: variable cost per unit
Divide monthly fixed costs by average sales
Add the two: full cost per unit

say: Third, add up all monthly fixed costs, including your own wage, and divide by the units you realistically sell in a month. Use your average, not your best month.

panel.heading: Full cost of one unit
items: List every variable cost for one batch
Divide by good units: variable cost per unit
Divide monthly fixed costs by average sales
Add the two: full cost per unit

say: Fourth, add the two. That is your full cost per unit.

panel.heading: Full cost of one unit
items: List every variable cost for one batch
Divide by good units: variable cost per unit
Divide monthly fixed costs by average sales
Add the two: full cost per unit

say: Burnt or broken items are not free. If a batch gives 48 good packs instead of 50, the good ones carry the cost of the bad ones.

panel.heading: Full cost of one unit
items: List every variable cost for one batch
Divide by good units: variable cost per unit
Divide monthly fixed costs by average sales
Add the two: full cost per unit
panel.rule: Divide by good units, not the number you planned.

say: Ngozi's batch of flour, sugar, margarine, eggs, oil, pouches, gas and her helper's pay costs 47,000 naira.
Divided by 50 packs, her variable cost is 940 naira a pack.
Her monthly fixed costs, including her own wage of 60,000 naira, total 110,000 naira. Shared over 200 packs, that is 550 naira a pack.
So each pack really costs 1,490 naira. Her old price of 1,500 naira leaves only 10 naira of profit.
Each sale first pays its own variable cost. What is left is the contribution margin. At 1,500 naira, Ngozi's contribution is 1,500 minus 940, which is 560 naira a pack.

panel.heading: How many must you sell?
items: Contribution = price minus variable cost
Break-even = fixed costs divided by contribution
Always round up to a whole unit
Margin of safety = expected minus break-even

say: Break-even is fixed costs divided by contribution. 110,000 divided by 560 is 196.4.

panel.heading: How many must you sell?
items: Contribution = price minus variable cost
Break-even = fixed costs divided by contribution
Always round up to a whole unit
Margin of safety = expected minus break-even

say: Always round up. Ngozi must sell 197 packs a month just to cover her costs and her wage. Only the 198th pack gives profit.

panel.heading: How many must you sell?
items: Contribution = price minus variable cost
Break-even = fixed costs divided by contribution
Always round up to a whole unit
Margin of safety = expected minus break-even

say: If she expects to sell 250 packs, her margin of safety is 53 packs, about 21 percent. Below about 10 percent, one bad week could push the month into a loss.

panel.heading: How many must you sell?
items: Contribution = price minus variable cost
Break-even = fixed costs divided by contribution
Always round up to a whole unit
Margin of safety = expected minus break-even

say: Use break-even to test a price. At 1,500 naira, Ngozi needs 197 packs a month.
At 1,700 naira, her contribution becomes 760 naira, and she needs only 145 packs. That is 52 fewer packs every month.
But never price below your variable cost. For Ngozi, any price under 940 naira loses money on every pack.
Markup is profit as a percentage of cost. A 30 percent markup on 1,490 naira gives 1,937 naira. But that is only about a 23 percent margin.
Margin is profit as a percentage of price. For a 30 percent margin, divide 1,490 by 0.70. That gives about 2,130 naira.
The market says similar packs sell for up to about 2,000 naira, so Ngozi chooses 1,700 naira for now and works to raise volume.
Here is how the mistake happens.
Funke's jar costs 2,000 naira, and she priced it at 3,000 naira. That is a 50 percent markup, but only a 33 percent margin.
A true 50 percent margin would need 4,000 naira. That is too high for her market, so she settles on 3,500 naira, about 43 percent. Now it is a conscious choice.
Shops need their own profit, so they buy at a lower price. If Ngozi sells to a shop at 1,400 naira, she still makes 460 naira contribution, and the shop resells at 1,700 naira.
Keep wholesale above variable cost, and set a minimum order so the lower price is earned by volume.

panel.heading: Setting a wholesale price
items: Keep it above your variable cost
Make a real contribution per unit
Set a minimum order, like 20 packs
Leave the shop room to profit

say: To remember. Full cost is variable plus fixed cost per unit. Break-even is fixed costs divided by contribution, rounded up. A small price rise can cut it sharply. Use the margin formula, not a markup, for a target margin.
And keep wholesale prices above variable cost.

panel.heading: Remember
items: Full cost = variable + fixed cost per unit
Break-even = fixed costs divided by contribution
A small price rise can cut break-even sharply
Target margin: price = cost / (1 minus margin)
Wholesale must stay above variable cost

say: Now cost one unit of your main product, find your break-even point and margin of safety, and price it with both markup and margin before you choose.
